question: Can you follow a melodic line through the changing hands and registers that carry it?
intro: The rippling surface of this miniature hides an intricate exchange between the hands: accompaniment and melodic notes cross registers without breaking the flow. Eugen d’Albert, who studied with Liszt, records it on an early Odeon disc.

cues.title: A surface made of crossings
cues.text: The written texture combines flowing semiquavers with shorter notes that move between registers. Listen for the melody within the ripples: the hands exchange positions, but the musical line need not sound broken into separate gestures.
cues.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au_bord_d%27une_source explains the crossed-hand pattern and its register changes. General score description, not a particular fingering claim about d’Albert.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A Swiss piece revised
cues.text: Liszt first writes the piece for Album d’un voyageur, then revises it for the Swiss book of Années de pèlerinage. The familiar 1855 form is not simply an unchanged sketch from the earlier collection.
cues.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au_bord_d%27une_source distinguishes the earlier Album d’un voyageur and revised Années versions.

cues.title: Keep the melody continuous
cues.text: Throughout the flowing passages, try following the longer melodic direction across the smaller notes. A change of register can move the line from below the figuration to above it without creating a new phrase.
cues.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Au_bord_d%27une_source describes alternating registers and intricate connecting scales/arpeggios. This is a general listening instruction.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A pupil records Liszt
cues.text: D’Albert studies with Liszt in Weimar in the early 1880s. That connection makes the disc a document of a pupil’s later interpretation, not an audio record of Liszt himself or proof that every detail reproduces the teacher’s playing.
cues.evidence: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/c.asp?c=C6; Eliot Levin’s biography documents d’Albert’s study with Liszt and later recording career.

cues.title: A larger central swell
cues.text: The recorded level rises strongly through this central span. Follow the melodic line through the increase in weight: the piece’s flowing surface can support a substantial crest without abandoning its basic motion.
cues.evidence: Analysis boundary 2:00; −13.3 dB at 2:00 rises to maximum −6.8 at 2:05, remaining strong through 2:20.

cues.title: The sound draws back
cues.text: The strong central span withdraws into a lighter one. Listen for continuity through the reduction of force rather than treating the change as a stop between separate pieces.
cues.evidence: Analysis boundary 2:28; level falls from −9.6 dB at 2:20 to −16 at 2:25 and −19.8 by 2:45.

cues.title: An Odeon side survives
cues.text: The reissue identifies Odeon 76565, matrix xxB 5732, and dates it 1912/3; the upload narrows that to March 1913. The dossier retains the distinction instead of treating a more precise filename as independent confirmation.
cues.evidence: Selected item’s Symposium 1146 track-list scan, track 4: https://archive.org/download/02-eugen-d-albert-syposium-1146/D%27Albert%20tracks.jpg; upload filename says III.1913.

cues.title: Let the ripples settle
cues.text: The final sounds fall away before the file ends. Listen through their decay rather than mistaking the remaining transfer silence for an extra musical pause inside the piece.
cues.evidence: Analysis: around −20 dB through 3:30–3:35, −55.2 at 3:40 and −69.6 at 3:45; file duration 3:48.7.

transitions.title: The flowing design gathers greater weight
transitions.how: The continuing figuration supports a larger central rise. Increasing dynamic weight and fuller register allow the melody to project through the rippling surface; continuity of motion connects the stronger span to the earlier design rather than interrupting it with a new movement.
transitions.evidence: Analysis boundaries 1:56 and 2:00; strongest windows 2:05–2:20. The general score description documents connecting scales and arpeggios.

transitions.title: The crest withdraws towards the close
transitions.how: The central weight diminishes while the flowing design remains the listener’s point of reference. Smaller gestures and reduced force carry the piece towards its ending, so the release comes through a shrinking scale rather than an abrupt break in its continuity.
transitions.evidence: Analysis boundary 2:28 and reduced levels after 2:25; final decay begins around 3:40. The precise version’s optional coda is not identified.

composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: The touring pianist who made a single theme change character, and eventually stripped virtuosity down to a few unresolved notes.
facts: Piano with Carl Czerny and composition with Antonio Salieri in Vienna; later composition with Anton Reicha in Paris
Weimar masterclasses; first president of the Hungarian Royal Academy of Music, founded in 1875
Piano music and transcriptions; thirteen symphonic poems; two programme symphonies; concertos, songs and sacred music
composer.background:
Liszt was born in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Hungarian kingdom, where his father Adam worked on an Esterházy estate. Hungary remained his declared homeland, although German and French were his principal languages. Adam taught him piano before taking him to Vienna in 1822 for lessons with Carl Czerny, who had studied with Beethoven, and Antonio Salieri. The family moved to Paris the following year. The Conservatoire refused him admission as a foreigner; private teaching and public concerts supplied his education instead. His early career therefore joined two institutions that would remain distinct in his adult life: the disciplined lesson and the commercial concert platform.

Adam died in 1827, leaving the sixteen-year-old Liszt to support himself and his mother by teaching. Paris offered an education beyond the keyboard: Victor Hugo, the religious social thinker Félicité de Lamennais, Chopin and Berlioz belonged to his intellectual or musical circle. Hearing Paganini in 1832 suggested that a pianist might make technical difficulty carry the same theatrical force as the violinist’s leaps and harmonics. Liszt responded with prolonged practice and transcription: his piano version of Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, published in 1834, aimed to preserve orchestral detail.
